chunks.text: Semal, also called the red silk-cotton tree (Bombax ceiba), belongs to the mallow family Malvaceae (order Malvales) and has 15 recognised synonyms, including the older names Bombax malabaricum and Gossampinus malabarica. It is native across a wide swathe of tropical Asia and Oceania — Pakistan, India, Nepal, Sri Lanka, Bangladesh, Myanmar, southern China, Taiwan, Thailand, Vietnam, Malaysia, Indonesia, the Philippines, the Solomon Islands, Papua New Guinea and northern Australia — typically in moist broadleaf forest, though in southern China it also grows in drier valleys and savannas. It reaches an average height of about 20 m, with wet-tropical specimens occasionally exceeding 60 m; young trees have conical spines on the trunk and limbs that wear away with age. Its palmate leaves have about six leaflets radiating from a central point, and its large, striking red cup-shaped flowers (7-11 cm wide, petals to 12 cm) open before new leaves appear in spring (roughly late February to early May), giving way to fruits that ripen from green to brown and split open to release seeds wrapped in soft, white, wind-borne cotton-like floss.

The tree's soft, fluffy seed floss is carded into thread and woven into textiles in Nepal and India, and used across North India as stuffing for pillows and mattresses; the wood itself is soft and not commercially significant as timber. In Thailand, the dried flower cores are used in regional dishes such as nam ngiao noodle soup and kaeng khae curry, and in parts of India the flower buds have historically been eaten as a vegetable. The tree attracts fruit-eating birds such as Japanese white-eyes as well as honeybees and bumblebees, and in Guangzhou (Canton) it is the city's official flower, inspiring the branding of China Southern Airlines and local transport operators, where elderly residents traditionally gather its fallen flowers for tea and soup.

chunks.source: Indian Forester / wisdomlib — Bombax ceiba folklore
chunks.text: In Indian tradition, semal occupies a complex mythological position: it has been revered since Vedic times as a 'god tree', yet in some regional folklore it is also called 'Yamadruma', the tree of Yama, the lord of death, and is regarded with a degree of dread as well as reverence. It plays a role in numerous socio-religious ceremonies, rites and festivals among tribal and rural communities across India. Notably, its wood and branches are traditionally burned during Holika Dahan, the bonfire ritual of the Holi festival in North India — a practice reported to be putting real pressure on semal populations in some regions (for example, an estimated 1,500-2,000 trees or large branches cut and burned annually around Udaipur, Rajasthan).
